subject: chemistry

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book states the rule as a bare possession statement ('an atom must possess eight electrons in its outermost energy level for its stability'); the card adds HOW atoms reach eight (losing, gaining or sharing), which is the NCERT form of the rule.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The rule
lines: Octet rule: atoms take part in bonding so
as to have eight electrons in their
They reach eight by losing, gaining or

steps.why: Eight outer electrons is the noble gas arrangement, the most stable one, so every bond in this chapter is explained as a route to eight.
common_mistakes: Writing eight electrons in the atom instead of eight electrons in the outermost shell.
Leaving out how atoms reach eight: by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.
steps.memory_tip: Octet means a set of eight. Eight outer electrons is the noble gas count.
steps.margin_note: The words outermost shell and eight electrons must both appear.

steps.label: The example
lines: Sodium loses one electron and chlorine
gains it. Both ions end with eight
steps.why: One worked example shows the rule in use: sodium reaches eight by losing an electron, chlorine by gaining one.
common_mistakes: Writing Na⁺ as 2,8,1 — the ion has lost its outer electron, so it is 2,8.
steps.memory_tip: Sodium gives one electron, chlorine takes it, and both end at eight.
steps.margin_note: Any correct example is accepted. NaCl is the shortest one to write.

insider_note: The two-mark answer is the rule plus one example with electron counts in brackets — the bracketed counts are what separate a full answer from a half answer.
